html:
Israel and Judah were two small Iron Age kingdoms in the southern Levant, in the hills of today's Israel and the West Bank, from about 1000 BCE until Judah fell to Babylon in 586 BCE. Their people, the Israelites, and their writings shaped Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

The name Israel first appears around 1208 BCE on the Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian victory monument. Archaeology suggests the Israelites grew out of the older Canaanite culture of the region.

The Bible tells of a united kingdom under Saul, David and Solomon, ruling from Jerusalem. Evidence for this united monarchy is thin and much debated, though an inscription from the ninth century BCE mentions a "House of David". What is clear is that by the ninth century there were two kingdoms:

  • Israel in the north, the larger and richer, with its capital at Samaria.
  • Judah in the south, smaller and poorer, ruled from Jerusalem by kings of the line of David.

Both lived in the shadow of great empires. Assyria destroyed Israel in 722 BCE and deported many of its people. Judah survived as an Assyrian vassal and withstood a siege by Sennacherib in 701 BCE. In 586 BCE Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple, and took many of its people into exile.

Exile did not end them. When Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, exiles were allowed to return and rebuild. In these centuries much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape, and with it the belief in one God at the heart of Judaism.
